source.title: Sparse Autoencoder Features for Classifications and Transferability
source.authors: J. Gallifant; Shan Chen; Kuleen Sasse; H. Aerts; Thomas Hartvigsen; D. Bitterman

record.tranche_reason: The study uses pretrained SAE features as inputs to classification and transfer experiments, but does not test superposition, feature geometry, capacity competition, or whether SAE features are canonical model units.
record.gate_note: The paper reports classification performance using SAE features, but those downstream scores do not test the superposition claims or establish that the SAE has recovered the model's underlying features. Table 6 separately reports overlap between top-20 features selected by classifiers trained under different language conditions; those overlap results are recorded as related feature-selection findings, not as tests of the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study applies pretrained Gemma Scope SAE features as inputs to logistic-regression classifiers and reports downstream F1 against hidden-state and TF-IDF baselines. It does not test toy-model geometry, capacity competition, origins of polysemanticity, whether SAEs recover the model's true features, feature completeness or stability, or feature dimensionality. The Table 6 overlap compares top-20 features chosen by classifiers trained on different languages. That measures task-feature selection, not stability or canonicality of SAE units. The reader's T4 classification is correct.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. More precisely: summation-then-binarization of pretrained SAE features beats hidden-state and TF-IDF baselines on most safety classification tasks. The features show cross-lingual (and preliminary cross-modal) transfer, and 2B SAE features can predict 9B-IT answer correctness. The authors leave semantic alignment of SAE features with human concepts, and robustness under domain shift, as open questions. They draw no conclusions about superposition.
record.recipe_differences: The study applies pretrained Gemma Scope SAEs to classification; it does not reproduce or test the original toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Classification performance varies with layer, pooling strategy, binarization, model, and training language; the paper reports middle layers often perform better and native-language training generally outperforms English transfer.

fits_no_version.finding: Top-20 classifier-selected SAE features overlap little across languages (Jaccard about 0.06–0.26), yet English-trained classifiers transfer with F1 up to 0.888 (RU, 9B) and 0.903 (RU, 9B-IT).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-relevant SAE features selected by supervised classifiers differ across input languages, even when cross-lingual transfer performs reasonably.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing Gemma Scope SAE width consistently lowers classification F1, most steeply without binarization (Appendix A.3, Figure 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider SAEs can reduce downstream linear-probe discriminability of aggregated SAE features.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The study uses only pretrained Gemma 2 SAEs for its main analysis. Its reported feature-overlap measure compares classifier-selected top features across language conditions, not repeated measurements of feature identity or completeness. The paper itself describes multimodal and cross-lingual evaluations as limited or preliminary.
record.rows_left_out: Classification F1 results and feature-overlap results outside Table 6 were not recorded because they measure downstream classifier utility or related evaluations, not the listed superposition and feature-unit claims.

untested.parts: All: toy models, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, sparsity transition, geometry.
All: capacity competition, importance-based dedicated dimensions.
Whether features are distributed across neurons or recoverable by SAEs. Pretrained SAEs are used without validating recovery; classification F1 is not evidence on this.
Completeness, stability across SAE training runs, and canonicality. Width effects (Appendix A.3) and cross-language overlaps concern classifier utility, not unit identity.

record.verdict_notes: All 16 rows correctly carry versions ['none'] with state cannot_determine. The study is not an original source, and no labels are warranted. The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition only in passing, in its related-work discussion of polysemanticity. Leaving out the F1 results is appropriate because they measure downstream utility.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometric arrangements.
Whether polysemanticity results from limited capacity or whether importance determines which features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons can arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The experiments use pretrained SAE activations but do not directly validate feature recovery or test whether features are distributed across neurons.
Completeness, stability, and canonicality of SAE features are not tested. The reported overlap concerns classifier-selected top features across language conditions.
The study does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.
